sum: The Annapurna Circuit with a three-day detour from Manang through Khangsar and across the landslide slopes to Tilicho Lake at 4,919 m, before crossing the Thorong La.
reach: By tourist bus (7–9 hours) or by air (about 25 minutes).

guide.note: Since April 2023 the Nepal Tourism Board has required foreign trekkers in conservation areas to walk with a licensed guide, though checks on the trail are inconsistent. A guide matters more on this detour than on the main circuit: the line through the landslide area changes every season, the base camp lodges need booking ahead, and someone has to judge the weather for both the lake and the pass.

access: Reach Besisahar by bus from Kathmandu in six to seven hours or from Pokhara in four to five, then take a shared jeep up the Marsyangdi road to Dharapani or Chame. The trek finishes at Jomsom, with early flights or a day-long road journey to Pokhara.

photo.a: A lone trekker stands beside a small tent on the gravel shore of bright blue Tilicho Lake, with snow slopes on the left and white clouds above bare brown mountains.

includes: porter in most packages (the cheapest tiers leave one out)
lodge beds and three meals a day on the trek
bus and shared jeep at both ends of the trek

permits.name: Annapurna Conservation Area Permit
permits.where: Online at NTNC's e-permit site, or in person at the Tourist Service Centre in Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, and the Nepal Tourism Board office in Pokhara. A permit issued at a trail checkpost costs double.

permits.name: Trekkers' Information Management System card
permits.where: Only through a registered trekking agency, which applies in the Nepal Tourism Board's online system with your route and your guide's details. Individual trekkers can no longer buy one over the counter.

transportText: Bus from Kathmandu to Besisahar and a jeep seat up the valley; at the end a flight or a jeep seat from Jomsom to Pokhara, and the tourist bus back to Kathmandu
tips: Pack light for the detour. You carry everything across the landslide slopes twice.
Use trekking poles and boots with a firm edge on the gravel traverse.
Take sunglasses, sunscreen and a windproof layer to the lake; the glare off ice and water is fierce.
Bring all the cash you need from Kathmandu or Pokhara. There is nowhere to get money beyond Chame.
If the weather turns at base camp, wait a day rather than rushing to the lake in cloud.

days.t: Drive to Besisahar, jeep to Dharapani
days.note: A long road day: bus to Besisahar from Pokhara or Kathmandu, then a shared jeep up the Marsyangdi on a rough track cut into the gorge wall. Sleeping at Dharapani rather than riding on to Chame gives you an extra day of gradual ascent on foot.

Mostly gentle climbing beside the river and the road, with one steep forest section between Danakyu and Timang where the footpath cuts off the road's bends. Manaslu is behind you at Timang, and Annapurna II comes into view before Chame. The hot springs across the river ease tired legs.

Through pine forest to the apple farm at Bhratang, round the foot of the Paungda Danda rock wall and up to Dhikur Pokhari for lunch. Cross the river to Upper Pisang rather than staying on the road: the view is better and it sets you up for tomorrow's high route.

days.t: Upper Pisang to Manang through Ghyaru and Ngawal
days.note: Climb the switchbacks to Ghyaru and follow the high trail through Ngawal before dropping to the valley floor and walking on through Braga to Manang. It is a long day, but being above 3,600 m at midday and sleeping lower is exactly what your body needs before the lake.

Two nights here are the minimum. Walk to Gangapurna Lake and up the moraine to the Chongkor viewpoint, then rest. Buy snacks for the days ahead, where lodges are basic, and ask lodge owners about the state of the landslide trail and whether the base camp lodges are open.

Leave the main circuit at the western end of Manang, drop to the river and climb to Khangsar, the last real village, for an early lunch. A steady hour and a half more, past a small monastery, brings you to the lodges at Shree Kharka. The sleeping gain is about 540 m, so walk slowly.

days.t: Shree Kharka to Tilicho Base Camp
days.note: The crux of the approach. After about an hour the path enters the landslide area: a narrow track across steep, loose gravel with rock pinnacles above and the river far below. Go early, before sun and wind start stones moving, keep gaps between people and do not stop. Base camp is on the valley floor beyond.

days.t: Tilicho Lake, then back to Shree Kharka
days.note: Start by five. The trail zigzags up the moraine for three to four hours to a crest a little higher than the lake, then eases down to the viewpoint above the shore. Leave by ten, when the wind rises, return to base camp for lunch and recross the landslide slopes to Shree Kharka.

A high traverse saves going back to Manang. The trail climbs past the ruins of old Khangsar to a shoulder with a long view down the Marsyangdi, drops steeply to a footbridge over the river and climbs to join the main circuit below Yak Kharka. There are no lodges on the way, so carry lunch.

Back on the main circuit: an hour to Ledar, a drop to the river, and a climb to a traverse where stones come down from the slope above. After the lake this height should feel comfortable. If it does not, wait a day here or lower before trying the pass.

days.t: Over the Thorong La to Muktinath
days.note: Start between four and five. Zigzags lead to High Camp, then a long climb over moraine and past false summits reaches the pass at 5,416 m, usually four to five hours from Phedi. The 1,650 m descent to Muktinath is steep and loose at first; go slowly and use poles.

Take the footpath that avoids the road: over a ridge south of Muktinath, steeply down to the Panda Khola and the Bon village of Lubra, then along the gravel riverbed to the Kali Gandaki and Jomsom. After heavy rain the riverbed can be impassable, and the road by Kagbeni is the fallback.

Morning flight to Pokhara if wind and cloud allow, or eight to ten hours by road down the Kali Gandaki through Tatopani and Beni. Flights are often cancelled, so do not book an international departure for the next day.
